Epistolarium — The Letters of Tycho Brahe

Charter. Epistolarium is the reading edition and apparatus of Tycho Brahe’s correspondence as the standard corpus prints it: the letters and acts of the Danish Society for Language and Literature’s digital re-edition (tekstnet.dk, 2019) of J. L. E. Dreyer’s Opera Omnia VI–VIII and XIV. Each document is given in its original Latin, German or Danish beside an English translation made for this edition by a language model and checked against Dreyer’s pages, with a one-sentence abstract, the parties identified against the Familia register, the place of writing, the date with its calendar, the edition of record by volume and page, the manuscript witnesses by kind, and its position in the exchange. It is the standard corpus, not the whole surviving correspondence: the letters published since Dreyer are listed, not edited, in §11.

508 documents (500 letters · 8 acts) · 1568–1601 · 283 issued by Tycho, 203 addressed to him, 22 between others · 138 correspondents · 439 with a manuscript witness, 69 in print only · 457 translations collated against Dreyer, 51 not · 61 places of writing

1Introduction

What this edition contains

The 508 documents here are the contents of Tycho Brahes Breve, the digital edition published by the Danish Society for Language and Literature at tekstnet.dk (redaktion Peter Zeeberg, 2019), which re-edits the letters printed by J. L. E. Dreyer in Tychonis Brahe Dani Opera Omnia: vol. VI (1919), the Epistolae astronomicae of 1596 re-edited; vol. VII (1924), the letters of 1568–1597; vol. VIII (1925), the letters of 1596–1601; and, from vol. XIV (1928), Epistolae et Acta, the letter-type documents the digital edition selected. Dreyer’s corpus is in substance the one F. R. Friis assembled between 1875 and 1909, with few additions (Norlind 1970, p. 175). The digital edition has 509 letter pages; two of them carry the same letter to Scaliger of 23 July 1600, which is counted once here. Of the 508, 500 are letters and 8 are acts of letter form — two printing privileges, a deed, three testimonials, a petition and a receipt — kept because the edition keeps them and marked as acts. Every document keeps its tekstnet identifier as its key and links to its tekstnet page, where the editors’ commentary and textual notes stand.

This is not the whole correspondence

It is the standard corpus. At least seven letters to or from Tycho and one letter about him have been published since Dreyer and are not in the edition: Tycho to Christoph Clavius, 5 January 1600 (Norlind 1954; Norlind 1970, Bilaga 9); Tycho to the Doge Marino Grimani, 28 November 1598 (Norlind 1970, Bilaga 7); the Liddel letters of 1587, the Ripensis letters of 1598, the Lund chapter’s letter of 1593 and Tengnagel’s letter to Rantzau of 1597 (Bilagor 2, 6, 4, 5); and the Danish documents in J. R. Christianson’s addenda to vol. XIV (Centaurus 16, 1972). They are listed with their prints and archives in §11, not edited. Whole correspondences are lost — Tycho’s letters to Vedel burned with Bishop Worm’s library in 1728, most of Rosenkrantz’s papers at Fredrikshald in 1826 — and no letter at all survives from 1569 or 1570 (Norlind 1970, pp. 174–175). No letter to or from Ursus, Wittich or Mercator exists; the Ursus quarrel ran in print. The digital edition’s own overview speaks of 350 letters, and Early Modern Letters Online catalogues the same printed corpus as 505; the differences are enclosures, testimonials, declarations and receipts counted or not, and the definitions table below says exactly what is counted here.

The texts

The Latin, German and Danish texts are tekstnet’s, read in 2026 against the page images of Dreyer’s printed volumes; defects of the first transcription were corrected, and every document whose printed words differ from a second transcription of the same tekstnet page lists both readings beneath the original on its letter page (80 documents; Dreyer’s page decides, and where the audit paragraph does not name the word that check has not yet been made). Dreyer’s volume and page are cited on every record, with a link to the page in the facsimile tekstnet serves. The 47 letters of the Hven–Kassel exchange survive only as Tycho printed them in his Epistolarum astronomicarum liber primus of 1596, edited by him for publication (Mosley, Jardine & Tybjerg 2003); their text is that of the print as Dreyer reprinted it, no manuscript is cited for them because the edition cites none, and the letters Tycho despatched to Kassel, which survive at Marburg (Hessisches Staatsarchiv, Best. 3 II Nr. 1070), are not collated here.

The English translations

The English was produced for this edition in 2026 by a large language model (Anthropic’s Claude) and is not the work of a human translator; no Latinist has reviewed it. Every translation was then read against the original in an independent pass, and 457 of the 508 documents were collated against the page images of Dreyer’s edition; the 289 defects that pass found — most of them in the transcribed originals rather than in the English — were corrected. 51 documents, 47 of them the Kassel letters of Opera Omnia VI, which the digital edition does not paginate, have not been so collated; each says so, and none is graded higher than Probable. The grade beside each translation — Secure, Probable, Possible — is the checker’s judgement of that translation’s fidelity to Dreyer’s printed text, given with its grounds on the letter page; it grades the English, not the Latin, the date, the attribution or the manuscript, and “Secure” means that a machine check against the page found no defect, not that a scholar has read it. Quote the original, not the English.

What the counts count

Direction follows the edited parties: 283 documents issued by Tycho, 203 addressed to him, 22 letters between other people, indexed under both. The receipt of 29 May 1601, whose addressee the digital edition leaves blank, is counted as addressed to him; the partition by tekstnet’s raw fields is given in the table for reconciliation with earlier citations. A correspondent is an entry in the Familia register — a person, a body such as the University of Copenhagen, or a group of unnamed recipients — reached through 149 name-forms of the edition; there are 138 such entries, and 4 documents have no addressee. A manuscript witness is one line of the edition’s own apparatus, whatever the manuscript is — an autograph, the sender’s draft, a contemporary copy or an eighteenth-century transcript; §5 separates the kinds by the edition’s wording, 146 documents survive only in copies, and “in manuscript” never means “in autograph”. The edition’s sigla A, B, C order the witnesses and have nothing to do with the grade words. A place of writing is the place named in the dateline, not the correspondent’s residence. The three periods are the editor’s, cut at 1 January 1577 and at Tycho’s departure from Hven on 29 April 1597.

Dates and calendars

Dates stand as the edition gives them, with the calendar the dateline names, [O.S.] or [N.S.]; the calendar conventions are stated in §8. 26 documents are dated only to a year or a month and are printed so. Where this edition dates a letter otherwise than tekstnet’s catalogue line (23 documents), both values and the basis are given on the record and in §8.

What the numbers are not

508 is the size of one edition, not the number of letters Tycho wrote or received; the letters per year measure what survives and what Friis and Dreyer printed. A correspondent’s count is not the size of the exchange. A repository’s count is of witness lines, including later copies. No figure on this page is a survival rate. Identity and biography are Familia’s, the itinerary is Loca’s, the printed books are Typographica’s; this edition links to them.

How to read this edition

The catalogue (§2) is one row per document, sortable and filterable, with the whole table downloadable as a spreadsheet. The register (§3) gives every document a record card in date order — parties, place, date, abstract, incipit, edition of record, witnesses, position in the exchange, translation grade — and each card leads to the letter’s own page, where the original stands above or beside the English with the apparatus and the audit’s warrant. The indexes (§4–§9) re-project the same records by correspondent, by manuscript, by print, by place, by year and by subject; the translations and their checking have their own section (§10); what is missing or doubtful is listed in §11; every source is described in §12. Each record prints its key, the tekstnet identifier (brahe-t_15680114001), and is addressable: #brahe-t_15680114001 as an anchor on this page, letters/brahe-t_15680114001.html for the letter. All 508 texts in one file, for searching the whole corpus without script, are at all.html.

2Catalogue of the documents

One row per document, in date order. Columns can be sorted by clicking their heading; the filters narrow the table and the count line says how many rows remain; the button exports the visible rows, and the whole table is letters.csv. Witness is the document’s witness class (§5); grade and collated are the translation’s (§10); kind separates the eight acts from the letters.

3Register of the documents

Every document as a record card, in date order under year headings, with everything known about it short of the text itself: the parties (linked to Familia), the place of writing (linked to Loca where Tycho’s own itinerary has the place), the date and its calendar, the abstract, the first words of the original, the editorial note where the letter needed one, the edition of record with Dreyer’s volume and pages and a link to the facsimile page, the manuscript witnesses by kind with a catalogue link where one is verified, the document’s place in the exchange, and the grade and collation status of the English. The text, the apparatus and the audit’s warrant are on the letter’s own page.

Hieronymus Wolf → Tycho Brahe — Augsburg

to TychoAbrahe-t_15711113001

17 May 1572 [O.S.]

Tycho Brahe → Johannes Pratensis — Herrevad

from TychoAbrahe-t_15720517001
Replies in hendecasyllabic verse cast as prose, expressing delight at Pratensis's letter and lamenting the displacement of true learning by scholastic barbarism.
Sequitur mea responsio, quae carmine constat hendecasyllabico instar prosae consignato.

Editorial note. The hendecasyllabic poem that the rubric announces — absent from the working transcription when this file was first made — has now been recovered and supplied from Dreyer, Opera Omnia VII pp. 9–10, taken from the digitised text. Long-s misreadings are silently normalised (suêre→fuêre, srugum→frugum); a stray footnote-anchor caret after Monstrabit is dropped; one genuinely uncertain word is flagged in the Apparatus (the subject is in "quas nunc is … intulêre Musis", where the plural verb wants a plural subject — ii/hi). The poem is a warm verse-letter answering Pratensis's of 7 May 1572: a humanist exhortation to scorn scholastic "Barbarism" and climb to the study of Earth and Heaven, then practical business — a prospective alchemical assistant ("that undaunted Dane"), the playfully mythologised delay in delivering felled timber ("despoiling the Nymphs," forbidden by Ceres until the harvest rites are done), and a request for distilling cucurbits from the potter Andreas.

Johannes Pratensis → Tycho Brahe — Copenhagen

to TychoAbrahe-t_15730416001
Reports on the gilding of Tycho's celestial globe — the goldsmith cannot lay gold stars on silver, the painter would smother the engraving — and urges an all-gold scheme with matt figures on a burnished ground, costed at four rose nobles; then on the printing of De nova stella, arguing Tycho out of the title-word Lucubrationes.
RECEPI literas tuas, TYCHO optime, quibus negotia tua promovenda apud Artifices tuos …

Editorial note. Published until now as lost. That was a transcription defect: the first transcription stored the editorial note that stands before this letter (Responsio ad has interijt…, which refers to a different, genuinely lost reply) and dropped the letter itself. The letter survives complete — TBOO VII pp. 10–13 — and is given here in full for the first time.

20 January 1587 [O.S.]

Tycho Brahe → Christoph Rothmann — Hven

from TychoBnot collatedbrahe-t_15870120001
Acknowledges Rothmann's April letter with its recondite astronomical discussions, explains the delay in replying, and reports having communicated celestial observations to the Landgrave.
QVAS ad me superiori Anno Mense Aprili, tum Mandato Illustrissimi Principis tui, tum …

Editorial note. The longest-but-one letter in the corpus and a cornerstone of the Tycho–Rothmann correspondence — a sustained scientific letter covering: the 1585-comet observation-comparison and its near-zero parallax; the Paul Wittich instrument-priority story (the parallel-slit sights, the transverse-point division from Homelius, the Nonius subtlety, the sextant); Petrus Ramus on "astronomy without hypotheses," refuted; refraction in detail (the 10-foot armilla; the star-refraction values; the Cygnus-tail / Algol discrepancy; the aether/air diaphaneity against Alhazen & Witelo); the great star-by-star demonstration that the fixed stars' latitudes vary with the changing obliquity (Spica as base, then Gemini, Capella, Orion, Regulus, Aldebaran, Altair, Antares, Libra, Sirius, Procyon); the 1584 lunar eclipse and the meridian-difference method; praise of Copernicus (and the Buchanan Sphaera); and the Frauenburg/Königsberg pole-elevations with Copernicus's own wooden triquetrum. Printed-edition text (clean), preserving v/u orthography as printed. One declared intervention: the digitised text layer-intruded apparatus "A" sigla on some 70 words are removed as non-textual (as in the letters to Scaliger of 23 Aug 1598, to Peucer of 1590 and 13 Sept 1588, to the Landgrave of 16 Aug 1588, to Herwart of 16 Nov 1599, and from Rothmann of 13 Oct 1588). Zodiac/planet glyphs (♈ ♉ ♊ ♍ ♌ ♎ ♏ ♐ ♑ ♒ ☉ ☽ ♂ ♃ ♄) are reproduced as transcribed. The dateline ("Vraniburgi 20 die Ianuarij, Anno 87") is Old Style (Danish Julian); it agrees with the catalogue label. Cross-check: page-collated against Dreyer's Opera Omnia, vol. VI pp. 86–104. The dense numeral spine is confirmed against the edition of record — of some 70 distinct numerals (the obliquity cluster pp. 87/94; the full Spica-based star-by-star latitude series pp. 94–99; the Frauenburg 54°22¼′ / Königsberg 54°43′ / Reinhold's 54°17′-26″-short poles p. 103; the 1584-eclipse timings H.11ᵐ12 / H.13ᵐ8 / H.15ᵐ0 + the Kassel/Rostock meridian reductions p. 100; the refraction values p. 92), every legible value matches. One flag: the derived ecliptic obliquity the transcription gives as 23°31⅓′ is arithmetically correct (62°13′20″ − 38°42′ = 23°31⅓′); Dreyer's print shows "31½" at that one spot, so Dreyer is the outlier there — keep the transcription's ⅓ (a reviewer should not "correct" it toward Dreyer). 16 August 1588 [O.S.]

Tycho Brahe → Wilhelm IV, Landgrave of Hesse-Kassel — Hven

from TychoBnot collatedbrahe-t_15880816001
Explains a delayed reply by missed courier opportunities and ongoing Venus observations, which he intends to compare with prior morning observations before writing more fully.
QVOD tardius tam Tuæ Celsitudinis expectatione, quam mea ipsius voluntate ad literas quas …

Editorial note. A published letter — one of the set Tycho himself printed at his Uraniborg press in the Epistolae astronomicae (1596) — and the locus classicus, on Tycho's side, of the "five-minutes controversy": the Landgrave's mathematician Christoph Rothmann had made the fixed-star longitudes about 5′ greater than Tycho's, and Tycho here defends his own values at length, tracing Rothmann's excess to refraction in the southern (low-altitude) half of the zodiac and to the reliance on the Sun/Venus too near the horizon. The text is clean (printed source) and preserves genuine early-modern v/u orthography (vt, vbi, varie, obseruatio), reproduced as printed. Two declared interventions in the source block: (1) the digitised text layer-intruded apparatus "A" sigla (footnote-anchors keying words to the apparatus) appended to some 25 words have been removed as non-textual (the same as in the Scaliger letter of 23 Aug 1598 and the undated Peucer letter of 1590); (2) the opening word's dittography "ILLVSTRISSIMOILLVSTRISSIMO" (the word transcribed twice) is reduced to a single ILLVSTRISSIMO (flagged). The zodiac glyph ♒ (Aquarius) is reproduced as printed. The dateline ("Vraniburgi, Die 16. Augusti, Anno 1588") is Old Style (Danish Julian); it agrees with the catalogue label. Cross-check: page-collated against Dreyer's Opera Omnia, vol. VI pp. 121–132. All cruxes confirmed: the 5′ longitude discrepancy (and "duodecima gradus portiuncula" = 5′); the 4-or-5′ refraction advancement and the 30°-altitude floor (p. 140); the reciprocal-Venus chronology 1582 / 1585 / 1587 / 1588 with the 17–18 Aug Venus–Jupiter conjunction sighted "from both heads of Gemini" (p. 143); the 5-year solar Ephemeris; the Copernicus/mid-Scorpio solar-apogee point (p. 140); and the dateline (p. 146). The flagged opening dittography is vindicated — Dreyer prints ILLVSTRISSIMO once (p. 135), so the reduction is correct.

13 September 1588 [O.S.]

Tycho Brahe → Caspar Peucer — Hven

from TychoAbrahe-t_15880913002
Opens a correspondence via Rantzau's introduction and undertakes to address Peucer's doubts about the diagram of Tycho's new world-system hypothesis conveyed through Rantzau.
HABEBAM iam dudum in votis tecum vel coram, cum Vitebergam olim transirem, vel etiam …

Text recovered. 17 words missing from inside this letter — dropped by a defective transcription of the source — have been restored from the text of record and translated into place.

Editorial note. A foundational document — Tycho's first long letter to Caspar Peucer (earlier than the undated reply of 1590), and the locus classicus of the autobiographical genesis of the Tychonic world-system: how, from a Leipzig boyhood with the cross-staff, through the deficiencies of both the Ptolemaic/Alphonsine and Copernican hypotheses, the Mars-parallax test of 1582 and the abandonment of the solid orbs (from the comets) led him to his geo-heliocentric arrangement. It also lays out the 7-book plan of his great Astronomical work, describes Uraniborg and Stjerneborg, casts (from old notes) Peucer's own horoscope, refutes Francisco Valles, and treats the Isaiah/Job fluid-heavens exegesis (overlapping the undated 1590 Peucer letter) and the Mars-parallax/system content (overlapping the Magini letter of 1 Dec 1590, the Landgrave letter of 16 Aug 1588, and the Hájek letter of 3 Aug 1590). Two declared interventions in the source block: (1) the digitised text layer-intruded apparatus "A" sigla (footnote-anchors to the witnesses) on some 90 words are removed as non-textual (as in the letters to Scaliger of 23 Aug 1598, to Peucer of 1590, to the Landgrave of 16 Aug 1588, to Herwart of 16 Nov 1599, and from Rothmann of 13 Oct 1588); (2) a genuine lacuna/anacoluthon in the source ("…circa Solem annua per totos orbes circumgyratione …" before "Habuit etiam quidam alius Mathematicus") is marked … and flagged. Greek (προσθαφαιρέσεων = prosthaphaereses; Phaenomeνων = φαινομένων) and the glyphs (☉ ☾ ☿ ♀ ♂ ♃ ♄ ♋ ♑ ♊ ♌; □ = square, △ = trine, ⚹ = sextile; M.C. = Medium Coeli) are reproduced as transcribed. The dateline ("Uraniburgi die 13. Septembris Anno 1588") is Old Style (Danish); it agrees with the catalogue label. Cross-check: page-collated against Dreyer's Opera Omnia, vol. VII pp. 127–141 (running head "TYCHO AD CASPARUM PEUCERUM 13 SEPT. 1588"). All cruxes confirmed: the solar parameters — apogee at the end of 6° Cancer, eccentricity 2° 9⅓′ (the contested ⅓ fraction read unambiguously at 12× zoom, p. 140); the 7-book plan (count and contents/order, p. 132); Peucer's horoscope (☿ in Capricorn 3rd house; ☾ in Gemini 9th; ♂ lord of 7th in 12th; liberation when the ☾-direction reaches ⚹♂ at 14° Leo in the M.C., "iuxta aetatis annum 60," pp. 137–138); the Uraniborg/Stjerneborg numerals (24-yrs' observations, "plura quam 20" instruments, the 7-crypt subterranean observatory, p. 139–140); and the Valles refutation — Dreyer genuinely prints "FRANCICUS VALLESIUS" (sic, for Franciscus), exactly as the transcription notes (p. 133).

13 October 1588 [O.S.]

Christoph Rothmann → Tycho Brahe — Kassel

to TychoBnot collatedbrahe-t_15881013001
Acknowledges both recent letters and the second tome of De mundi aetherei, then argues persistently that the celestial matter is elemental air and not aether.
ACCEPTATISSIMÆ mihi fuerunt vtræque tuæ literas, Nobilissime ac Præstantissime D. TYCHO, …
Dating dateline "13. Calendas Octobris"

Editorial note. A capital document in the history of cosmology: Christoph Rothmann's long reply to Tycho, defending three theses — (i) the matter of the heavens is pure air, not a distinct aether (a sustained optical argument from refraction, citing Alhazen and Witelo); (ii) comet tails are of the head's own matter, self-luminous, and do not point at the Sun (proved from the Landgrave's record of the 1558 comet in Leovitius's Ephemerides); and (iii) an unreserved defence of Copernicanism against Tycho's "new hypotheses," which Rothmann reads as merely "inverted Copernicus." Printed-edition text (clean), preserving genuine v/u orthography (vt, vbi, RefractionemA→Refractionem), reproduced as printed. Two declared interventions in the source block: (1) the digitised text layer-intruded apparatus "A" sigla on some 30 words are removed as non-textual (as in the letters to Scaliger of 23 Aug 1598, to Peucer of 1590, to the Landgrave of 16 Aug 1588, and to Herwart of 16 Nov 1599); (2) one transcription slip obseruamus for observatus (in the 1558-comet quote) is left in the source and rendered correctly. Greek (φιλαληθέια, ἀυτόματον), the planet/zodiac glyphs (♍ ♈), and Rothmann's coinage Homocentrepicyclepicyclis are reproduced as transcribed. Dateline crux (named, not smoothed): the source reads "Cassellis 13. Calendas Octobris, Anno salutis M.D.LXXXIIX" (= 1588). Taken strictly as Roman dating, a.d. XIII Kalendas Octobris = 19 September; the catalogue/edition resolves it to 13 October (the form is anomalous — "Calendas" without "ante diem," a known looseness/printer's rendering). The header gives the catalogued 13 October with the literal dateline shown; the discrepancy is flagged in the Apparatus. As a Lutheran-Hesse letter it is Old Style (Julian). Cross-check: page-collated against Dreyer's Opera Omnia, vol. VI pp. 151–161, Epistolarum astronomicarum Liber Primus. All citations and numerals confirmed: Alhazen 7.2/7.4 + Witelo 10.3 + the 52-radii / 1:100000 / 1:140608 figures (p. 151); Witelo 10.10/10.8 + refraction 1½′/3′ (p. 152); Euclid I.21 (p. 153); twilight 16½° / 24° (p. 154); the 1558-comet positions (pp. 155–156). The dateline is verbatim Dreyer: "Caßellis 13. Calendas Octobris … M. D. LXXXIIX" (p. 161) — Dreyer himself prints no "ante diem," confirming the anomaly the apparatus flags; the "13 October" resolution is the catalogue's. Two text-layer/print notes: (a) in the second Alhazen citation (book 7, ch. 7), the chapter digit did not survive digitised text layer (book 7 is legible); the ch.-7 reading is secure on the surrounding citation-series but cannot be confirmed from the digitised text layer alone; (b) obseruamus est in the 1558-comet quote is Dreyer's own printed reading (he daggers it †) — see the reframed intervention-note below.

1590

Tycho Brahe → Caspar Peucer — Hven

from TychoAbrahe-t_15900000001
Explains the delay in replying: Bongars, a French envoy who delivered Peucer's second letter in Copenhagen, departed for Germany before Tycho could send a reply.
CUM paulo ante nostratia, quæ quotannis circa Solstitium Æstivum celebrantur, Comitia …

Editorial note. One of Tycho's longest and most important letters of cosmological–theological argument: his reply to Caspar Peucer on (i) the nature and substance of the heavens (no solid orbs; not per se luminous; not "fiery"), (ii) the "waters above the firmament" — a sustained refutation of the supercelestial-waters reading of Genesis 1, with Hebrew exegesis and patristic/reformer authorities, (iii) the Milky Way and the New Star of 1572 as condensations of celestial matter, (iv) the wholly celestial matter of comets (against being made of exhalations), (v) metals/alchemy ("terrestrial astronomy"), (vi) Venus and Mercury, and (vii) Rothmann's Copernicanism. Two declared interventions in the source block: (1) the working transcription is densely peppered with digitised text layer-intruded Dreyer apparatus sigla — a stray superscript "A" (the footnote-anchor keying a word to witness A) tacked onto some 90 words, plus a couple of stray "" footnote-markers — these are non-textual and have been removed (not silently normalised; the same treatment as in the Scaliger letter of 23 Aug 1598). (2) The transcription lost or garbled the Hebrew: Dreyer prints the actual Hebrew lemmata of the Genesis/Psalms discussion, but the working text renders most as "XXX" and one as a scrambled fragment (עיקד for רקיע). Each lost lemma is editorially supplied in [square brackets] from the unambiguous context (the standard text of Gen 1:6–7, Ps 104, Jer 10/51) and itemised in the Apparatus; one analogical word-pair Tycho cites as a grammatical parallel is genuinely illegible and marked […]. Two short transcription lacunae (in the alchemy and Craig-Apologia sentences) are marked …. Dating: the letter carries no dateline (it ends simply "Vale"); the catalogue assigns 1590 (the label reads "1590. empty"), consistent with the internal evidence — the Apologeticum against Craig "not yet received," the Epistolae astronomicae and Progymnasmata Tome I in preparation, Bongars's embassy, and Peucer "freed in old age from so many hardships" (released from his Crypto-Calvinist imprisonment in 1586). Header leads with the catalogued year, flagged undated. Cross-check: the reply was located and collated — Dreyer, Opera Omnia vol. VII pp. 228–234, running head "TYCHO AD CASPARUM PEUCERUM 1590," source-line "[Ex exemplo Hauniensi excerpsit Langebek. 178]." (An earlier pass had found only Peucer's inbound letter of 10 May 1589 at Dreyer pp. some 170–177; the reply sits some 50 pp. later.) The Latin context — Uranoscopium, the Castalio/Pagninus/Moses citations, the aquae supercaelestes refutation, Gen 1, Jer 10, Ps 104/18 — collates and matches the working text. One residual limitation, on the Hebrew alone: Dreyer does print the Hebrew lemmata at pp. 232–234, but the digitised text renders the Hebrew glyphs as Latin-script garbage, so the supplied forms (raqiaʿ רקיע, shamayim שמים, mayim מים) cannot be verified against Dreyer's type from the digitised text — they rest on the confirmed Latin context, the fixed biblical text, and the surviving transcription mayim*; a definitive glyph-check needs a reading of the page images. The argument's through-line is secure.

Text recovered. The postscript or enclosure, missing from the first transcription, has been restored from the text of record and translated. The Source and English columns below are now complete.

Editorial note. This is a letter to Tycho — Hájek's long reply to a (now-lost or separately-transmitted) Tycho letter of the previous year, the major document of the Tycho–Hájek comet-motion controversy and the earliest surviving notice (in the correspondence) of Tycho's Mars-parallax result and of his completed reply to John Craig. The working transcription is clean; a small number of obvious digitised text layer slips in the transcription have been kept verbatim in the source block and corrected in the translation, flagged in the Apparatus (fint→sint, verilate→veritate, reprensionem→reprehensionem, the stray space in parallaxium,). The Greek transliteration dedomenis (δεδομένα, "the data") and the glyphs ♂ ☉ ♀ ☿ ♊ are reproduced as transcribed. The dateline ("11. Iunij novo stylo, qui dies fuit feria secunda Pentecostes Anno 1590") is explicitly New Style and self-dates correctly: in the Gregorian calendar Whit Monday 1590 was indeed 11 June; agrees with the catalogue label. Cross-check: page-collated against Dreyer's Opera Omnia, vol. VII pp. 258–268 (running head "THAD. HAGECIUS AD TYCHONEM 1/11 IUN. 1590"; main letter from cod. Vindob. lat. 10686.66 = witness A, with a POST SCRIPTA on p. 268 from cod. Vindob. lat. 10686.14 = witness B — both sigla vindicated). Every load-bearing reading confirmed: the Mars-at-opposition parallax notice (p. 260, qualitative — no numeric value attached), the comet-motion-law thesis and Tycho's difficulty-vs-impossibility counter (p. 262), the Craig/Apologetica responsio praise (pp. 265–266; Dreyer prints the name CRAIGIUS / CRAIGIJ, not "Craigo" — that form belongs to a Brucaeus letter at p. 359), the technical sidebar (24 Nov / 26 Jan / 15′, p. 265), and the dateline + Hayck signature (p. 268). The page image garbles IACOBUS CURTIUS→"PACORUS CURTIUS" (p. 260) and feria→"serra" (p. 268); both are page image artifacts, not variants — the transcription's readings are correct.

Editorial note. Tycho's direct reply to Hájek's letter of 11 June 1590: a point-by-point rebuttal of Hájek's thesis that comet-motions cannot be reduced to law, plus the new Caesarean Privilege (via Curtius), the Craig papers, instrument models, the paper-mill publication delay, and the 21 July 1590 solar eclipse (the same eclipse, book-returns, and prosthaphaeresis crux that recur in the Magini letter of the same period, 1 December 1590). The transcription is comparatively clean (only light digitised text layer slips, corrected and flagged; no heavy apparatus-sigla as in Hájek's letter of 11 Jun 1590 or the undated Peucer letter of 1590). Greek-inflected forms (Phaenomenωn = φαινομένων; Dedomena/Dedomenis = δεδόμενα) and the glyphs (♂ ♀ ☿ ☉ ♄ ♃ ♌; ☉lem = Solem, ☉lis = Solis) are reproduced as transcribed. The dateline ("Uraniburgi die 3. Augusti stylo veteri Anno 1590") is explicitly Old Style; it agrees with the catalogue label. Cross-check: page-collated against Dreyer's Opera Omnia, vol. VII pp. 264–275 (running head "TYCHO AD THADDAEUM HAGECIUM 3 AUG. 1590"). All cruxes confirmed: the comet daily-motion figures (1577 comet 6°→¼°/day, book 2 ch. 8, p. 278; the Feb–Mar 1590 comet 7½°→1½°/day over 12 days, ⅛ of a circle, "3rd column" of the table, p. 279); the prosthaphaeresis dates 24 Nov / 26 Dec (with the "pag. 279" cross-ref and "two whole months," pp. 283–284); the 1577-not-1580 correction of Hájek's slip (p. 282); the Craig/Regiomontanus parallax (Problems 2/3/4, the 18-minute interval, p. 285); the 21 July 1590 eclipse (6ʰ51ᵐ / 9ʰ exactly / 4 of 8 digits / Leo, p. 289); and the production notes (5–6 artificers, 3rd year, 3+5 gatherings, chs. 7/9/10, two papermakers, Apian's comet of 1531, p. 287–288). Dreyer also prints a short closing CURTIO postscript (p. 275) that the source block folds into the body.

Text recovered. The postscript or enclosure, missing from the first transcription, has been restored from the text of record and translated. The Source and English columns below are now complete.

Editorial note. One of the most important scientific letters in the whole correspondence: Tycho's full, programmatic reply to Magini on (i) the Mars-parallax / fluid-heavens argument, (ii) the Tychonic world-system, (iii) the deficiencies of the Alphonsine/Copernican/Prutenic restitutions, (iv) the critique of Werner's De motu octavae sphaerae, (v) Magini's own Theoricae, and (vi) the constancy of terrestrial latitudes against Domenico Maria Novara — argued with a reproduced Regiomontanus 1462 Rome observation table. The edition names Tabulae Primi Mobilis as the source edition (Magini printed Tycho's letter there); Dreyer's Opera Omnia vol. VII is cited as the edition of record by the edition's convention The transcription is clean; a few obvious digitised text layer slips are kept verbatim in the source block and corrected in the translation, flagged in the Apparatus (inaequalitales→inaequalitates, exactura→exactiora). The Greek-inflected forms (Phaenomenωn = φαινομένων; Tecmirijs = τεκμηρίοις) and the glyphs (♂ ☉ ♀ ☿ ♍ ♋ ♑ ♒) are reproduced as transcribed. The dateline ("Calendis Decembris, Anni veteris Iuliani 1590") is explicitly Old Style (Julian); it agrees with the catalogue label. Cross-check: page-collated against Dreyer's Opera Omnia, vol. VII pp. 295–298 (running head "TYCHO AD IOAN. ANT. MAGINUM 1 DEC. 1590"). All 16 cells of the Regiomontanus 1462 table match Dreyer to the arcsecond — including the day-11 corrected altitude 27°51′50″, which proves the +1′ raw→corrected wrinkle (see Apparatus) is Dreyer's own reading (the source-print's), not a transcription artifact; the reproduce-with-flag handling is vindicated. The prose cruxes match too: Rome 41°54′, Sun-centre 48°6′ (p. 297); Venice 45°16′, Ancona 44⅙°=44°10′ vs neoterics 43⅔°=43°40′, Domenico Maria's drift 1⅙°=1°10′, Copernicus's Frauenburg error 2¾′ (p. 298); the eclipse 6ʰ51ᵐ / 9ʰ00ᵐ / 4-of-8 digits (p. 296). Dreyer prints the Ancona/Domenico-Maria figures as vulgar fractions; the translation renders them as exact fraction→minute conversions.

from TychoAbrahe-t_15911114001
Challenges Craig for falling silent in their ongoing dispute, arguing that acknowledging errors is praiseworthy and urging him either to concede or to continue the debate.
QUID cunctaris, mi CRAIGE, curque tam cito pedem referens nusquam amplius appares? Si …

Editorial note. Tycho's major polemical letter in the Tycho–Craig comet controversy, and a documentary nexus: to convince the Aristotelian Scot that the learned world has already conceded the comets are aethereal, Tycho quotes verbatim, at length, five other letters he had received — two excerpts from Jacob Curtius (Kurz von Senftenau) (Prague, 28 June 1590), the whole Craig-paragraph of Hájek's letter (= his letter of 11 June 1590, here re-quoted with minor textual variants) plus a later Hájek concession (Prague, 29 Aug 1591), and three excerpts from Magini (to Gellius Sascerides, 8 July 1590; again to Gellius; and to Tycho himself, 13 Sept 1590 — the very letter Tycho answers on 1 December 1590). The embedded Hájek paragraph is rendered here consistently with Hájek's letter of 11 June 1590, following this witness's own wording where it diverges (noted in the Apparatus). The source uses » « guillemets for the quotations; digitised text layer line-break splits inside the Curtius quote (privile gium, d e Cometis, er uditis, eo s, contr a, vo lunt) are reproduced verbatim in the source block and read as the obvious whole words in the translation. The Greek (ἀμαθηματικός, ἄθεος) and the glyph-plus-ending forms (♂tis = Martis, ♂tem = Martem, ☉lem = Solem) are reproduced as transcribed. The dateline ("Uraniburgi 14. Novembris Anno 1591") is Old Style (Danish Julian); it agrees with the catalogue label. Cross-check: page-collated against Dreyer's Opera Omnia, vol. VII pp. 308–319 (running head "TYCHO AD IOANNEM CRAIGUM 14 NOV. 1591"). All five embedded quotations are present and correctly attributed (Curtius ×2, Hájek ×1 long + 1 short concession of 29 Aug 1591, Magini ×3); the dateline (p. 319) and the MS witness are confirmed — Dreyer prints the head-note "[Ex apographo in codice Vindobonensi lat. 9737 f]", vindicating both the 9737f shelfmark and the apograph/copy characterisation. One transcription slip, now resolved: in Magini's second excerpt the working transcription reads "pag. 218" for the correct "pag. 281" (a digit transposition). The figure is a cross-reference to Tycho's De mundi aetherei (1588): the original 1588 marginal page-number 281 appears at exactly the "Cum igitur nunc constet Angulus BHK" passage (Dreyer, Opera Omnia IV p. 233; p. 247 of the digital file). So 281 is correct; the translation follows it.

Dating begun 30 November 1592 [N.S.]

Editorial note. The longest letter in the whole corpus and the last of the Tycho–Rothmann correspondence (Rothmann, ill since his 1590 visit to Hven, never replied; the exchange ends here). After a condolence on Rothmann's illness and an account of why the comet-works remain unpublished, the bulk is a sustained, point-by-point demolition of John Craig (the unnamed "Scot") and his anti-Tychonic Capnuraniae restinctio — defending the comets' aethereal nature, the 1572 nova, and, notably, John Dee (Nucleus parallaticus) and Thomas Digges (Alae), with embedded quotations from Jacob Monau, Craig himself, Hájek, and Curtius. It closes with the Mars/Venus-eccentricity argument against Copernicus and the 1000-star catalogue. Printed-edition text (clean), v/u orthography retained. Declared interventions: the digitised text layer-intruded apparatus "A" sigla on some 40 words removed as non-textual (as in the letters to Scaliger of 23 Aug 1598, to Peucer of 1590 and 13 Sept 1588, to the Landgrave of 16 Aug 1588, to Herwart of 16 Nov 1599, from Rothmann of 13 Oct 1588 and 20 Jan 1587, and to Hájek of 3 Aug 1590). Greek (ἀυτὸς ἔφα, πολυρρητορείαν [src πολυροτορέιαν], κάπνἐγκέφαλος, λόγῳ) and the glyphs (♂ ♀ ♊ ♋ ☉ ☽) are reproduced as transcribed; the long quotations from Craig (and from Monau/Hájek/Curtius), italic in the print, are kept inline and identified in the Apparatus. Dating crux (named). The header dateline is "Vraniburgi die 14. Ianuarij Anni 1595" (Old Style); but the letter embeds its own composition note — "Hodie, qui est dies ultimus Novembris Anni 1592 novo stylo" (30 Nov 1592 N.S., when Tycho received Rothmann's 28 Sept letter and Craig's screed via the Magdeburg courier) — so it was begun late 1592 and only completed/sent in Jan 1595. The header gives the catalogued/dispatch date with the internal note flagged. Cross-check: page-collated against Dreyer's Opera Omnia, vol. VI pp. 319–337. All cruxes confirmed: the internal composition note "Hodie, qui est dies ultimus Novembris Anni 1592 novo stylo" (the Magdeburg-courier receipt of Rothmann's 28 Sept letter, p. 334) and the header dateline 14 Jan 1595 (p. 337) — the dual-date is genuine; the Craig title Capnuraniae restinctio, seu Cometarum in Aethera sublimationis refutatio (p. 320); the defence of John Dee in suo Nucleo Parallatico and Thomas Digges alas (p. 330); the embedded Monau / Hájek-+-Curtius quotations (pp. 323, 334); the four Greek terms (heavily garbled in the page image but located in place); and the Mars/Venus-eccentricity coda (Mars ecc. "vel potius nonnihilo maior," Venus apogee 17° Gemini vs init. Cancer, p. 336) + the 1000-star note (p. 337).

Editorial note: the working transcription is heavily peppered with digitised text layer-intruded Dreyer apparatus sigla — a stray superscript "A" (the footnote-anchor keying a word to witness A) tacked onto dozens of words. These are non-textual and have been removed from the source block below (declared, not silently normalised). Two readings were cross-checked against the local Dreyer Opera Omnia page image (vol. VIII): (1) "fusile" in the first sentence of the Ptolemy paragraph is a corruption of "fuisse" (the long-s ligature fuiſſe mis-resolved; the parallel clause later reads fuisse plainly, and the sense requires it) — translated as fuisse; (2) "centenis 30" (Ptolemy's precession rate) is the printed Dreyer reading and is reproduced verbatim — it is a genuine textual crux (see Apparatus), since Ptolemy's published value is 1° per 100 years. Greek (κοσμοπολίτην, Parallaxεων, πρόποδος, pragmatεία) and zodiac glyphs (♈ ♉ ♊ ♋ ♌) are reproduced as transcribed. The dateline ("die 23. Augusti st. vet. … 1598") agrees with the catalogue label.

Direction note. Incoming letter — from the jurist-poet Hartwig von Dassel (Hardewigus Dasselius), a kinsman/friend of Heinrich Rantzau, to Tycho. A humanist consolatio: a jeremiad on the age, and a eulogy for Heinrich Rantzau — Tycho's Wandsbek host — who died 1 January 1599. Survives in Dassel's own printed Poemata + Epistolae (no manuscript witness).

Direction note. Incoming letter — from Johannes Kepler to Tycho — Kepler's apologia for his earlier flattering letter to Ursus, which Ursus had printed in his defamatory De astronomicis hypothesibus (1597) and weaponised against Tycho. Place not given (Graz, where Kepler then was); dated only to February 1599 (the edition gives no day). The text as the edition transmits it ends without valediction or date.

16 November 1599 [N.S.]

Tycho Brahe → Johann Georg Herwart von Hohenburg — Jiřice

from TychoAbrahe-t_15991116001
Acknowledges receipt of two letters and the Bavarian library catalogue, explaining his delayed reply by his busy correspondence while sending his eldest son to retrieve instruments from Magdeburg.
NOBILIS et Magnifice vir, amice plurimum honorande, utrasque tuas, eodem tenore ad me …

Editorial note. A long, three-stranded letter to the Bavarian Chancellor Herwart von Hohenburg (companion to Tycho's reply of 28 Aug 1600): (i) the exile/patronage narrative — the instruments' transport from Magdeburg down the Elbe, Rudolf II's favour through Barvitius, and the plague-flight from Benátky to Girsitz; (ii) a dense technical argument that the obliquity of the ecliptic is essentially constant (the ancients merely imprecise), with precession at 51″/yr, the year-length against Copernicus, and the solar eccentricity; and (iii) the celebrated prosthaphaeresis-priority story — Rheticus → Werner → Wittich → Bürgi → an unnamed "scurrilous sycophant" (Ursus) → Clavius, plus the Bavarian-library book-requests and the Leovitius/Fugger manuscripts. Two declared interventions in the source block: (1) the digitised text layer-intruded apparatus "A" sigla (footnote-anchors) on some 55 words are removed as non-textual (as in the letters to Scaliger of 23 Aug 1598, to Peucer of 1590, and to the Landgrave of 16 Aug 1588); (2) the source's square brackets around three late passages (the book-list, the Augsburg-youth/Fugger recollection, and the closing) are retained as printed — they are Dreyer's/the witness's editorial brackets (passages with witness-B divergence), flagged here; not this edition's. Greek (μικροκόσμῳ), the quadrature glyph □ (= quadraturis), and the planet/zodiac glyphs (♀ ☿ ☾ ☉ ♂ ♄ ♃ ♋ ♌ ♎ ♐ ♊) are reproduced as transcribed. The dateline ("ex arce Caesareana Girsitza 16. die Novembris stylo renovato Anno 1599") is explicitly New Style (stylo renovato); it agrees with the catalogue label. Cross-check: page-collated against Dreyer's Opera Omnia, vol. VIII pp. 209–217 (running head "TYCHO AD IOH. G. HERWARTUM 6/16 NOV. 1599"; from cod. Vindob. lat. 10702). The entire numerical spine is confirmed against the edition of record (not merely internally consistent): obliquity 23°31½′ (p. 209); precession 51″/yr = 1°/70½ yr, with the al-Battānī-derivation 1006 yrs = 14°15′ and 705 yrs = 10° (p. 212); year 365ᵈ 5ʰ "non plane 49ᵐ" (p. 212); solar eccentricity 2½ → al-Battānī/Asrael 2;5 → Tycho 2;9 (p. 213); the full al-Battānī/Asrael/Prophatius/ancients/moderns authority-and-value series incl. the ancients' 23°51⅓′ (pp. 211–212); the Rheticus→Werner→Wittich→Bürgi→Ursus→Clavius priority chain ("fere 20 annos," Wittich "anno 80 per 4 menses," pp. 214–216). One digitised text layer-watch: the Vultur volans declination the transcription gives as 5⅚° appears in the page image as the garbled "P. 51" (p. 210) — the ⅚ was lost in digitised text layer; the transcription's 5⅚° is the correct reading (consistent with the derived latitude 29°40′ that follows), not a variant.

14 April 1601 [N.S.]

Tycho Brahe → Martin Brasch — Prague

from TychoAbrahe-t_16010414001
Sends a copied excerpt on the history of astronomy and directs Brasch to Apian's Astronomicum Caesareum, Reinhold's tables, and Peucer's Sphaera for further sources, leaving composition of a poem to his discretion.
NULLA tui oblivione nec mea negligentia accidit, eruditissime Domine BRASCHI, quod Mag. …
Dating "the new Imperial Uraniborg"

Note. Continues the Brasch exchange (cf. brahe-t_16000915001). The body is Tycho's own outline for an epic poem, the History of Illustrious Astronomers — including seven lines of Tycho's hexameter verse and (at the end) the earliest naming of the Rudolphine Tables in this corpus. Recipient = Martin Brasch (Martinum Braschium); see the name note at brahe-t_16000915001.

4Correspondents

One entry per party to the correspondence, as the Familia register identifies them: 138 entries — 130 persons, 4 bodies and 4 groups of unnamed recipients — reached through 149 name-forms of the edition, which are printed beneath each name. The summary table gives the extent of each exchange in both directions, its span, its languages and how its documents survive; the entries below it list each exchange in order with the abstracts and the reply chain. Letters between two other people are indexed under both parties, and the one address naming two men (Valkendorf and Friis) counts under both entries, so the column sums exceed the number of documents. Who these people were is Familia’s to say; the name links there.

5The manuscript witnesses

What survives of the letters as objects, by the edition’s own witness lines. tekstnet gives each document up to three witnesses with the sigla A, B, C — a city, an institution, a shelfmark, sometimes a word saying what the manuscript is. This section keeps those lines as they stand, classes each by the edition’s wording, gathers them by repository and by shelfmark, and links the catalogue record where one is verified. Where the edition marks nothing, the line is unmarked: most unmarked Vienna and Basel lines are originals or drafts, but the edition does not say so and this section does not guess.

The kinds of witness

Kind of lineLinesBy the edition's wording
original36the edition writes Original, Originalbrev, Original letter or Autograf
draft38Kladde or koncept: the sender's draft
copy165Afskrift, transcript, excerpt, Langebek's Diplomatarium, a copy written into a printed book
unmarked236no such word; the edition's silence, not a finding

Per document, the classes below partition the 508 documents. The 36 with an original-marked witness are a floor set by the edition's wording, not a count of surviving autographs.

Witness classDocumentsDefinition
has an original36at least one witness line the edition marks as an original or autograph
drafts only36every witness line is a draft (Kladde)
copies only146every witness line is a copy: a contemporary copy, Langebek's eighteenth-century transcripts, an excerpt
unmarked only216the edition's lines carry no word saying what the manuscript is
mixed5lines of more than one kind, none marked original
no witness (print only)69no witness line; the letter survives in print (the 1596 Epistolae for the Kassel letters)

How the archives formed

Tycho kept his letters at Uraniborg, probably in a letter-room of their own together with his drafts, and planned to continue in print the collection he had begun with the Kassel letters in 1596; the itinerant years after 1597 — Rostock, Wandsbek, Wittenberg, Benátky — gave him no chance to keep the archive together, and much of it was probably lost then (Norlind 1970, p. 172). The largest part of what remained is in the Österreichische Nationalbibliothek in Vienna, where it arrived, so far as is known, at about the time the Fugger library came from Augsburg in 1656; it holds letters to and from Tycho in original and in draft, and the originals of his own letters to Hagecius, which Hagecius sent back at Tycho’s request for the planned continuation (pp. 172–173).

The Universitätsbibliothek Basel holds two folio volumes from the eighteenth-century collection of Werner Huber, catalogued in 1789, sold after his death and bought by the university in 1806 from the bookseller Johannes Schweighauser: one with forty original letters to Tycho (one of them to his sister Sophie), the other with eighty-four drafts of his own letters, most from his last two years (p. 173). The originals of his letters to Giovanni Antonio Magini came to the private archive of the Marchesi Malvezzi de’ Medici in Bologna, bought on a piazza there by the marchese’s great-grandfather, and were edited by Favaro in 1886 (p. 173). The Universitätsbibliothek München has, among the papers of the Bavarian chancellor Herwart von Hohenburg, originals from Tycho and Herwart’s drafts in reply (p. 173).

The Rosenkrantz family archive at Rosenholm held Tycho’s letters to Holger Rosenkrantz; Jacob Langebek had them copied in the mid-eighteenth century, and the copies are in Rigsarkivet in Copenhagen. The archive itself passed by inheritance in 1802 to the foreign minister Niels Rosenkrantz and then to his brother at Fredrikshald in Norway, where it burned in 1826 (pp. 173–174). Twenty-two letters from Tycho and three drafts from Rosenkrantz survive in Langebek’s copies, some of them in cipher (p. 179); that is why every Rosenkrantz witness in this edition is a copy. Other collections are gone: Bishop Christen Worm’s fifty or so letters from Tycho to Vedel, burned in the Copenhagen fire of 1728; the letters Søren Lintrup owned, probably lost in the Bergen fire of 1702; and the Tycho letters once in the Trew collection at Erlangen, which the catalogue lists but the collection no longer holds (p. 174). Few original letters by Tycho exist at all; most survive only in copies, some were written by an assistant and only signed by him, some were sent in duplicate by different routes (p. 176).

6Editions of record and concordance

Where each document was printed, and where its text here comes from. tekstnet names for every document the print it took the text from: Dreyer’s Opera Omnia for most, but for 133 documents an earlier print — Tycho’s own Epistolae astronomicae of 1596, Friis’s two editions of the learned correspondence (1876–86 and 1900–09), Favaro’s Magini letters, and a scatter of seventeenth- and eighteenth-century collections. The summary table folds those names to their prints; the concordance gives every document its Dreyer volume and pages, its first print and its tekstnet page.

The Hven–Kassel exchange 47 by the print · 49 by correspondent

The exchange with Landgrave Wilhelm IV of Hesse-Kassel and his astronomer Christoph Rothmann is the one part of his correspondence Tycho published himself, as Tychonis Brahe Dani Epistolarum astronomicarum libri, quorum primus (Uraniborg 1596; Nielsen 430), edited for print — passages cut, wording adjusted, the sequence arranged (Mosley, Jardine & Tybjerg 2003). Dreyer re-edited the book as Opera Omnia VI. Two definitions of the set therefore coexist and are tabled here: the letters whose source is the 1596 print, the source’s own unit; and the letters exchanged with Wilhelm IV, Rothmann and, after Wilhelm’s death, Landgrave Moritz, an editorial grouping that reaches into the exile years. The letters Tycho despatched to Kassel survive in the Hessisches Staatsarchiv Marburg, Best. 3 II Nr. 1070, the Landgrave’s correspondence with Tycho of 1585–1592, described with digital images in Arcinsys; which letters of the exchange the convolute holds has not been read letter by letter, and no witness line of the edition points to it, so it is stated here at convolute level and never as “this letter’s original”. The book itself is Typographica’s: its record and the census of its copies are linked.

Calendars

Denmark, Hesse-Kassel and the Lutheran north kept the Julian calendar until 1700; the Catholic lands adopted the Gregorian reform in 1582 and Bohemia in 1584, so from 1599 Tycho himself dated in New Style. The two calendars were ten days apart. The edition marks the style where the dateline or the editors give it — [O.S.] and [N.S.] in the headings here — and the table below shows how the marks fall by place of writing. A reply from Prague can therefore appear to precede the letter from Hven it answers; the register keeps the dates as given and does not convert them.

9Letters concerning the press

The documents that touch the making, gift, sale or acquisition of Tycho’s printed books — the paper and the press on Hven, the privileges, the presentation copies, the bookseller, the plates. The flag is the editor’s, set by reading the letters; no per-letter work is recorded, so the table cannot be grouped by book, and the criterion is a desideratum (§11). The books themselves are Typographica’s.
